# CEO Review: AI Assistant Plan

I don't know your vertical, your customers, or what data you hold, so I've flagged assumptions where they matter. The questions at the end could change my recommendation.

## 1. Premise Challenge

**"An AI assistant in the product" is the wrong unit of ambition.** A chat sidebar is table stakes, and every competitor will ship one within two quarters. Foundation models improve for free, so anything that is a thin wrapper gets commoditized by the next model release.

The better question is: **what job do your customers hire you for, and can AI do that job instead of helping them do it?**

- **Assistant:** answers questions, drafts text, and summarizes things. Value is incremental, and users compare it to ChatGPT.
- **Agent/teammate:** takes a goal, works across your system of record, and delivers a finished outcome for review. Value is a step change, and it can't be replicated without your data and workflows.

The 10x version is the second one.

## 2. The Options Spectrum

Four engineers for one year is roughly 4 engineer-years. That is enough for one real bet plus a foundation, not a portfolio.

| | **A. Copilot Sidebar** | **B. Embedded AI Features** | **C. Workflow Agents** | **D. Autonomous Teammate / Platform** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **What it is** | Chat over docs and data | AI woven into 5-8 existing flows (autofill, summarize, classify, suggest) | Agents that complete 2-3 high-value multi-step workflows end to end, with human approval | Agent that owns a function, proactive, cross-system, extensible by customers and partners |
| **Eng cost** | ~1 eng-year | ~2 eng-years | ~3-4 eng-years | 6+ eng-years (not fundable as stated) |
| **Differentiation** | Low | Medium | High | Category-defining, if it works |
| **Risk** | Looks like everyone else | Death by a thousand features, no narrative | Reliability and trust, with a narrow initial scope | Overreach, unreliable, and you run out of runway |
| **Pricing power** | Bundled, maybe a 10-15% upsell | Retention lever | New SKU, usage or outcome-based | Pricing model shift |

**Recommendation: C, built so it can grow into D.** Option A as a launch vehicle is fine if it's cheap, but it shouldn't consume the team.

## 3. What the 10x Version Looks Like

1. **It does the work.** Instead of "ask me how to reconcile this," it reconciles, flags the three exceptions, and asks you to approve.
2. **It's proactive.** It notices things ("this renewal is at risk and here's the draft outreach") rather than waiting to be asked.
3. **It learns each customer's way of working.** Corrections, approvals, and edits become per-account memory and tuned behavior. Switching costs rise with every use.
4. **It prices on outcomes.** Seat-based pricing caps your upside when AI reduces seats needed. Charge for work completed or value delivered.
5. **It's an interface for others.** Over time, customers and partners can build on top of it (tools, skills, integrations), which makes it a platform.

## 4. What Would Make It Category-Defining

Models won't be your moat. These will be:

- **Proprietary workflow data.** You see how work actually gets done, including decisions, corrections, and exceptions. Competitors with only the model can't see this. Instrument it from day one.
- **A closed feedback loop.** Every accept, edit, or reject becomes eval data and training signal. The product should get measurably better per customer each month.
- **Trust as a feature.** Permissions, audit trails, explainability, undo, and confidence-based escalation. In B2B this is often what wins the deal, not capability.
- **Owning one workflow completely.** Be the best in the world at one job before expanding. "AI for everything" is a feature. "The AI that closes your books in 2 days" is a category.
- **Distribution you already have.** You have customers, and a 40-person company can ship to them faster than a startup can acquire them. Use that.

## 5. Proposed Staffing and Timeline

**Team (4 engineers):**
- 1 on eval, observability, and guardrails. This is the most commonly underinvested role and the one that determines whether you ship something trustworthy.
- 2 on agent/workflow development (tools, orchestration, integration with your core product)
- 1 on UX, human-in-the-loop flows, and the feedback and data pipeline (a strong full-stack engineer with design partnership)

**Timeline:**
- **Months 0-2:** Pick the workflow. Interview 15-20 customers, pull usage data, and choose the job with the highest frequency, pain, and your-data advantage. Build the eval set *before* the agent. Ship an internal prototype.
- **Months 2-5:** Design-partner beta with 5-10 customers. Human-in-the-loop on everything. Measure task completion rate, edit rate, and time saved.
- **Months 5-9:** GA of workflow #1 with a pricing experiment. Start workflow #2 using shared infrastructure.
- **Months 9-12:** Proactive behavior, per-account memory, and an extensibility surface (internal tools API, maybe an early partner program).

**Kill/continue gates:**
- Month 3: Can the agent complete the workflow correctly more than 70% of the time on your eval set? If not, narrow the scope or change the workflow.
- Month 6: Are design partners using it weekly without being nagged? Would they pay? If not, stop and rethink.

## 6. Risks and What I'd Worry About

- **Reliability gap.** 90% accuracy feels great in a demo and is unacceptable in production for financial, legal, or operational work. Design around this with approvals, confidence thresholds, and scoped autonomy.
- **Scope creep.** Sales will ask for "AI for X" in every deal. Say no to everything outside the chosen workflow until it's working.
- **Inference cost.** Model that cost into unit economics early. Agentic workflows can use 10-100x the tokens of chat.
- **Platform risk.** Don't lock into one model provider. Abstract the model layer and keep your evals portable.
- **Incumbent response.** If a large competitor bundles AI for free, your advantage must be depth in the workflow, not the existence of AI.
- **Security and compliance.** Enterprise buyers will ask about data handling, tenant isolation, and SOC 2 implications on day one.

## 7. What I'd Cut

# CEO Review: AI Assistant Plan

I don't know your product, vertical, or data yet, so I've stated my assumptions and listed the questions that would change my answer at the end.

## 1. Challenge the premise

**"An AI assistant in the product" is a solution, not a strategy.** A chat sidebar is what every competitor will ship this quarter, so it can't be category-defining. The question is: **what work do your customers do in your product that they hate, that is expensive, and that you could do for them?**

The best framing is to stop selling software that helps people do a job and start selling the job done. Your 10x version follows from that.

## 2. Constraints that shape the answer

- **4 engineers for 12 months** is about 48 engineer-months. You can't compete on models, and you shouldn't try.
- **Your moat is not the AI.** Everyone has the same foundation models. Your moat is the workflow, the proprietary data, the customer trust, and the distribution you already have.
- **You're a B2B company with existing customers.** That is your unfair advantage over AI-native startups. They have better demos, and you have the context, permissions, integrations, and contracts.

## 3. Options, from conservative to ambitious

| | **A. Answer engine** | **B. Embedded intelligence** | **C. Workflow agent** | **D. System of action (10x)** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **What it is** | Chat over docs and customer data | AI woven into existing screens: drafting, summarizing, classifying, suggesting | Agent completes a multi-step task with human approval | Agents own one end-to-end outcome; humans supervise by exception |
| **Eng cost** | ~6 eng-months | ~15 eng-months | ~30 eng-months | ~45+ eng-months, narrow scope |
| **Differentiation** | Low, a checkbox feature | Medium, hard to copy without your UX | High, requires your data and integrations | Very high, a new product category |
| **Risk** | Low, but it won't move revenue | Medium | High: trust, evals, edge cases | Highest: you could overbuild before learning |
| **Business impact** | Marginal retention | Engagement and upsell | New pricing tier, real expansion | Outcome-based pricing, new buyer, new TAM |

## 4. The 10x version

**Pick one high-value workflow in your product and make it autonomous end-to-end.**

Don't build an assistant that can do a little of everything. Build the thing that does one job better than a human team, fully, with your customers' data, permissions, and approval rules.

The 10x version has five properties:

1. **Outcome-defined, not feature-defined.** "Closes your month-end reconciliation" or "resolves tier-1 tickets," not "ask questions about your data."
2. **Acts, not just answers.** It writes to systems, sends things, and triggers workflows, with permissioning and an audit trail.
3. **Learns from every correction.** Each human edit or approval becomes training signal in your eval set and your prompts and retrieval. Over time this is a data flywheel competitors can't replicate without your customers.
4. **Trust is a product feature.** Confidence scoring, explainability, "show your work," undo, role-based controls, and SOC 2-friendly logging. In B2B, trust infrastructure is the moat.
5. **Priced on outcomes.** Per resolved case, per processed document, or per task completed. That changes the buyer from IT budget to ops/line-of-business budget and sets you apart from "AI add-on" pricing.

## 5. What makes it category-defining

- **You own the system of record plus the system of action.** AI-native startups have the agent but not the data. Incumbents have the data but a bolted-on assistant. You can have both.
- **Your eval set is your real asset.** Hundreds of real, labeled, customer-validated examples of "good" in your domain compound over time.
- **Autonomy is earned progressively.** Suggest, then draft, then act with approval, then act autonomously by category. Customers dial it up as trust builds. This is the adoption path in risk-averse B2B.
- **You change the unit of value.** Customers stop asking "how many seats?" and start asking "how much work did it take off my team?"

## 6. Recommendation

**Build toward D, but ship through B and C. Don't skip to the end.**

**Quarter by quarter, with 4 engineers:**

- **Q1: Foundations and a wedge.** Pick the workflow. Ship a narrow embedded AI feature (option B) in it to 5-10 design partners within ~90 days. Build the eval harness and logging from day one, because that is the real infrastructure.
- **Q2: Move to supervised actions.** The AI drafts and executes with human approval. Instrument acceptance rate, edit distance, and time saved.
- **Q3: Selective autonomy.** Auto-approve the high-confidence categories. Add permissioning, audit trail, and the admin controls enterprise buyers require. Test outcome-based pricing with design partners.
- **Q4: Generalize and launch.** Productize the pattern, announce, and set up the second workflow on the same agent infrastructure.

**Team split:**
- 1 engineer: evals, observability, and model and prompt infrastructure
- 2 engineers: the workflow product (UX, agent logic, integrations)
- 1 engineer: data, permissions, security, and platform plumbing

Hire or contract design help. The UX of supervising an agent is the hardest and most underrated problem here.

## 7. What kills this plan

- **Spreading thin.** Four engineers can build one great workflow or five mediocre ones.
- **No evals.** If you can't measure quality, you can't ship autonomy, and the project turns into prompt whack-a-mole.
- **Inference cost eats margin.** Model unit economics per task before you commit to outcome pricing.
- **Trust incidents.** One bad autonomous action at a key customer can set you back a year. Build undo and approval gates first.
- **Model vendors move up the stack.** Mitigate by owning workflow, data, and integrations, and by staying model-agnostic.
- **Building in a vacuum.** If you don't have design partners by month 2, stop and reassess.

## 2. Foundational decisions

- **FND-01 ★** Define a single system of record for each entity: customer, subscription, usage, invoice, payment, ledger. Document ownership boundaries.
- **FND-02 ★** All monetary amounts are stored as integer minor units with an explicit currency code and an explicit per-currency exponent. Never use floats.
- **FND-03 ★** All timestamps are stored in UTC. Each customer has an explicit billing timezone for period boundaries.
- **FND-04 ★** Domain data is **append-only and event-sourced where money is concerned**. Corrections are new records that reference the originals.
- **FND-05 ★** All write APIs are idempotent (client-supplied keys).
- **FND-06 ★** Every record is tenant-scoped (legal entity, environment: live/test/sandbox).
- **FND-07** Every calculation must be **deterministic and reproducible** from versioned inputs (usage + price version + tax rules + FX rate).

## 3. Product catalog and pricing model

### Requirements

  - maximum cap / spend ceiling
  - free tier / included allowance (per period, one-time, or rolling)

  - one-time fees (onboarding, setup)

- **CAT-05** Tier computation scope is configurable: per subscription, per account hierarchy, per period, per commit term, or cumulative lifetime.

- **CAT-12** Grandfathering rules for legacy plans.

## 4. Metering

### 4.1 Event model
- **MET-01 ★** Usage event schema: `event_id` (unique, idempotency key), `customer_id` / `account_id`, `meter_id` / event name, `quantity` (decimal), `event_timestamp` (when it happened), `ingest_timestamp` (when received), `properties` (typed key-values), `source`, `schema_version`.
- **MET-02 ★** Attribution hierarchy: organization → account → project → API key → end-user (optional). Rollups are supported at every level.
- **MET-03** Quantity supports fractional decimals with a defined precision.
- **MET-04** Schema registry for event types, with validation and versioned evolution. Unknown properties are handled by policy (reject, quarantine, or store).

### 4.2 Ingestion
- **MET-10 ★** Ingestion is **at-least-once with deduplication**, yielding effectively-once billing. Dedup key is `(tenant, event_id)` with a defined dedup window (or unbounded for billing-grade).
- **MET-11** Ingestion paths: HTTP batch API, streaming (Kafka/Kinesis/PubSub), SDKs, gateway-native plugin, and file/object-store import for backfill.
- **MET-12** Ingestion is decoupled from the API serving path. Billing outage must not cause API outage (fail-open), and metering must buffer durably (no loss).
- **MET-13** Backpressure, rate limits, and per-tenant quotas on the ingestion API.
- **MET-14** A dead-letter/quarantine queue for invalid events, with tooling to inspect, fix, and replay.
- **MET-15** Ingestion latency target: events visible in aggregates within N seconds (define for portal vs. billing).
- **MET-16** Raw events are stored durably and immutably for the retention period required for disputes and audits.

### 4.3 Aggregation
- **MET-20** Aggregation functions: sum, count, count-distinct (unique), max, min, last, average, time-weighted average (e.g. provisioned GB-hours), and percentile (e.g. 95th) as a *should*.
- **MET-21** Aggregation windows: billing period, calendar day/hour (for rollups and caps), rolling windows, and per-event (for per-request pricing).
- **MET-22** Filters and group-by on event properties, so one raw stream can feed several meters.
- **MET-23 ★** Meter definitions are versioned. Changing a definition must not silently alter already-invoiced periods.
- **MET-24** Unique-count meters (e.g. monthly active users) must define cross-period semantics.
- **MET-25** Gauge/state meters (provisioned resources) support start/stop events and interval computation.

### 4.4 Late, out-of-order, and corrected data
- **MET-30 ★** Distinguish **event time** from **ingest time**. Periods are assigned by event time.
- **MET-31 ★** Define a **late-arrival policy**: a grace window before a period is closed/finalized. After finalization, late events are (a) billed on the next invoice, (b) trigger an adjustment/credit note, or (c) are written off. The policy is configurable per meter or customer.
- **MET-32** Corrections are done via compensating events or explicit adjustment records, never by mutating or deleting raw events.
- **MET-33** Backfill/replay tooling that is idempotent and shows a diff of the financial impact before commit.
- **MET-34** Clock-skew protection: reject or flag events with timestamps too far in the future or past.

### 4.5 Reconciliation and integrity
- **MET-40 ★** Automated reconciliation of metered usage against an independent source (gateway logs, upstream provider bills, data warehouse). Variance thresholds raise alerts.
- **MET-41** Gap detection: missing sequence numbers per source, or heartbeat events from emitters.
- **MET-42** Per-period **usage statement** that can be reproduced exactly from raw events.
- **MET-43** Usage export (CSV/JSON/API) at event or aggregate granularity for customer disputes.

### 4.6 Real-time controls
- **MET-50** Near-real-time usage and spend estimate per customer, project, and key.
- **MET-51** Budgets and alerts: customer-defined thresholds (50/80/100%), notified via email/webhook.
- **MET-52** Hard caps/soft caps: enforcement signal to the API gateway (throttle or block when limit reached). Define consistency tolerance (small overage permitted).
- **MET-53** Quota/entitlement checks exposed via low-latency API for the gateway, with caching and a defined staleness bound.
- **MET-54** Anomaly detection for usage spikes (fraud, runaway loops), with optional auto-pause.

### Open questions
- **Q4.1** Where is usage originally captured: API gateway, application service, or both? Which is the billing source of truth, and what happens on disagreement?
- **Q4.2** What is the acceptable error tolerance? Is 0.01% under- or over-billing acceptable, or must it be exact?
- **Q4.3** How long is the late-arrival window (hours, days)? Who absorbs the cost of late usage that arrives after invoice finalization?
- **Q4.4** Do events need to be signed or authenticated per source to prevent tampering or customer-side spoofing (relevant if customers self-report usage)?
- **Q4.5** Do customers report usage to you (customer-side metering) or only you observe it?
- **Q4.6** Is metered usage ever deleted? (GDPR/erasure vs. financial retention conflict; see Section 20.)
- **Q4.7** How granular must real-time visibility be, and does it need to be exact or an estimate?
- **Q4.8** What is the enforcement model when a hard cap is hit: reject requests, degrade, or allow with overage? Who owns that decision, billing or gateway?
- **Q4.9** Do usage-event properties contain PII or customer content? If so, what minimization is needed?
- **Q4.10** Expected cardinality of property values (affects storage and query cost for group-by).

## 5. Rating (usage → money)

- **RAT-01 ★** Rating is a pure function: `(usage aggregates, price version, discounts, commitments, FX) → priced line items`. It must be re-runnable and produce identical results.
- **RAT-02 ★** Rating output stores the **inputs used** (price version IDs, usage snapshot hash) so any line item is explainable.
- **RAT-03** Supports **streaming/incremental rating** for real-time spend estimates and **batch rating** for invoice finalization. Both must reconcile.
- **RAT-04** Application order is explicit and documented: allowance → tiers → minimums → discounts → credits/commit drawdown → tax.
- **RAT-05** Rounding rules are configurable, deterministic, and documented (per-unit vs per-line, round-half-even vs half-up).
- **RAT-06** Multi-meter bundles: shared allowances, "whichever is greater" logic, blended pricing.
- **RAT-07** Commit drawdown: usage consumes prepaid/committed balance first, with overage billed at defined (possibly different) rates.
- **RAT-08** Rerating: ability to re-rate a closed period with corrected prices or usage, producing a delta (credit/debit) rather than rewriting history.
- **RAT-09** Rating dry-run for "what-if" analyses and price-change impact analysis.
- **RAT-10** Currency conversion: rate source, rate timestamp, and locking policy (at invoice creation, at usage time, or contractual fixed rate).

- **Q5.3** What FX source and policy? Who bears FX risk?
- **Q5.4** Are there usage-based prices that depend on a third-party cost (pass-through pricing)?

## 0. Verdict

The target architecture is sound and conventional. The risk is in the plan's framing: **"do it once and do it right" is the riskiest part.** A big-bang rebuild of a system that touches every product surface, with legal exposure (consent, unsubscribe) and a reputation asset (email and SMS sender reputation), tends to fail by shipping late, missing undocumented behaviors of the old system, or causing a duplicate or missed-send incident during cutover. - **"Pluggable provider layer"** is speculative unless you have at least two real providers per channel on day one. Otherwise you'll design the abstraction around one vendor's quirks.

## 1. Questions that change the design

1. Peak and average volume per channel? Largest single fan-out (one event to N users)? Whether it's 10/sec or 10k/sec decides most of the infrastructure choices.
2. Which messages are **critical** (OTP, password reset, security alerts, payments) versus **bulk** (marketing, social)? This drives queue isolation and the rate-limit bypass policy.
3. Multi-tenant (you send on behalf of customers) or single-brand? Multi-tenant adds per-tenant isolation, sender domains and quotas.
4. Regulatory scope: GDPR, CAN-SPAM, TCPA, CASL, data residency?

## 2. Target design

### 2.1 Pipeline

```
Producers ──► Ingest API / domain-event consumer
                 │  (validate, authn, idempotency key, outbox)
                 ▼
          Durable log: `notification.requests` (partitioned by recipient_id)
                 ▼
          Orchestrator
            1. resolve recipient (profile, locale, tz, devices)
            2. choose type/category → channel plan
            3. check suppression + preferences + consent
            4. dedupe / collapse
            5. rate limit / quiet hours / digest decision
            6. emit per-channel delivery intents
                 ▼
     ┌── priority queues per channel (critical | default | bulk) ──┐
     ▼             ▼              ▼              ▼
  Email worker  SMS worker   Push worker   In-app writer
  render→send   render→send  render→send   store + realtime
     ▼             ▼              ▼              ▼
  Provider adapters (SES/SendGrid, Twilio, APNs/FCM, internal)
     ▼
  Provider webhooks ► Webhook ingester (verify, normalize) ► `delivery.events` log
                                                     ▼
                                       State updater + Analytics sink (warehouse)
```

### 2.2 Core decisions

| Decision | Recommendation | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Producer contract | A notification *request*: `{type, recipient, payload, idempotency_key, priority, ttl}`. Optionally a routing layer maps domain events → requests. | Avoids every domain team embedding channel logic. Mapping domain events directly couples the schema of every event to templates. Start explicit, add event mapping later. |
| Delivery semantics | At-least-once end to end, with idempotent consumers keyed by deterministic `delivery_id = hash(request_id, channel, recipient, version)` | Exactly-once doesn't exist across a provider boundary. |
| Dual-write safety | Transactional outbox in producers (or the ingest API writes to its own DB, then relays) | Otherwise "committed order but no notification" or the reverse. |
| Partitioning | By `recipient_id` | Gives per-user ordering, rate limits and digest accumulation without distributed locks. Cost: hot-key risk (§5). |
| Priority isolation | Separate queues and **separate worker capacity** per priority, not just a priority field | A marketing blast must never delay an OTP. |
| Preference evaluation | At **send time** (in the worker or just before), not only at enqueue | Delays, retries and digests create a gap in which a user may have unsubscribed. |
| Rendering | Render in the channel worker; **persist the rendered snapshot** (or hash plus template version) | Auditability, "what did we actually send?", and safe retries. |
| Provider layer | Adapter interface with a capability descriptor (max payload, supports batch, supports idempotency key, rate limits, webhook format) plus a routing policy (primary, fallback, weight) | Don't assume a lowest common denominator. |
| In-app | A separate store (inbox) plus a realtime fan-out (SSE/WebSocket), not "just another provider" | Read/unread state, pagination, counts and retention make it a product feature. |

### 2.3 Data model (sketch)

- `notification_request` (id, type, recipient, payload ref, idempotency_key, priority, created_at, expires_at)
- `delivery` (delivery_id, request_id, channel, provider, state, attempts, rendered_ref, provider_message_id, timestamps). State machine: `PLANNED → SUPPRESSED | DEFERRED | QUEUED → SENDING → SENT → DELIVERED | BOUNCED | FAILED | EXPIRED`, plus `OPENED`/`CLICKED` as events, not states.
- `delivery_event` (append-only, from providers and internal)
- `preference` (user, category, channel, state, **source, timestamp, consent text/version**), plus global quiet hours and tz
- `suppression` (address/device, reason: hard bounce, complaint, unsub, STOP, invalid token; scope)
- `template` / `template_version` (type, channel, locale, content, schema of required variables, status, author)
- `device` (user, platform, token, last_seen, invalidated_at)
- `digest_bucket` (user, digest_key, window, items, flush_at, state)
- `inbox_item` (user, id, payload, read_at, created_at, TTL)

Treat the **state machine and event log as the source of truth**. Analytics are derived from it.

## 3. Failure modes

### Ingestion and orchestration
- **Duplicate requests** (producer retries): idempotency store needs a TTL longer than the longest producer retry horizon. Store outage means either fail closed (reject) or accept duplicates; decide per priority.
- **Producer loops**: an event handler that triggers an event that triggers a notification can send a million emails. Needs per-producer and per-type circuit breakers and a global kill switch.
- **Fan-out amplification**: one request to 5M recipients overwhelms the orchestrator. Needs a separate bulk fan-out stage, throttled and resumable (checkpointed cursor).
- **Poison messages** (malformed payload, missing recipient): per-message retry cap, DLQ with tooling to inspect and replay. DLQ that nobody watches is a silent-loss mechanism.
- **Schema drift** between producers and templates: validate payload against the template's variable schema at ingest, not at render time.
- **Recipient resolution failure** (profile service down): defer with backoff. Never fall back to stale contact data for sensitive messages.
- **Wrong-recipient bugs** (e.g. email changed mid-flight, shared device, reassigned phone numbers): resolve the address at send time and for security messages re-verify. Recycled phone numbers will text strangers.

### Preferences, consent, rate limits
- **Stale preference cache** delivering after unsubscribe. This is a legal issue, so cache TTL must be short or invalidated on write for unsub/STOP events.
- **Preference migration without provenance**: you can't prove consent later.
- **Rate-limit store down**: fail open for critical, fail closed for bulk. Document this explicitly.
- **Rate-limit semantics**: are suppressed messages dropped, deferred or digested? "Dropped" silently loses important notifications. Define per type.
- **Critical-bypass abuse**: teams will mark everything critical. Needs an allowlist and a review process.
- **Quiet hours and tz**: missing tz, DST transitions, users who travel. Deferred messages that exceed TTL should expire, not send at 3pm as "your ride is arriving."

### Digests
- **Double flush or missed flush** (scheduler leader failover): flush must be idempotent (state transition `OPEN → FLUSHING → SENT` with CAS).
- **Stale content**: the digest says "3 new comments" but two were deleted. Re-hydrate or validate at flush.
- **Unbounded buckets**: cap items, and say "and 200 more."
- **Digest vs. realtime interaction**: user gets a realtime push and then the same item in a digest. Needs a per-item "already notified" marker.
- **Late-arriving item** during flush: goes in the next window, which must be handled deterministically.

### Rendering
- **Template bug shipped to everyone**: needs staged rollout (percentage or canary recipients), preview and lint in CI, instant rollback to the previous version.
- **Template injection (SSTI/XSS/header injection)**: sandboxed engine, auto-escaping, and no user-controlled content in subject or headers without sanitization.
- **Missing variable / locale fallback** renders "Hi {{name}}" or an empty body. Fail the render, don't send.
- **Channel constraints**: SMS segmenting (GSM-7 vs. UCS-2 emoji triples cost), push payload ≤ ~4KB, email clipping at ~102KB in Gmail, and dark-mode and client rendering quirks.

### Providers
- **Provider outage or brownout**: circuit breaker with failover. **Failover causes duplicates** if the primary accepted but timed out. Accept that and make it explicit; for OTP this is fine, for receipts it may not be.
- **Ambiguous timeouts**: request sent, no response. Use provider idempotency keys where supported; otherwise there's an irreducible duplicate-vs-loss choice.
- **Error classification** (permanent vs. transient vs. throttled): getting this wrong means either retry storms on hard bounces or dropped sends on transient errors.
- **Retry storms after recovery**: jittered backoff, plus a global concurrency cap per provider.
- **Webhook problems**: forged callbacks (verify signatures), out-of-order events (a `delivered` arriving after `bounced`; make state transitions monotonic), duplicates, burst delivery, and your endpoint being down (providers retry for limited windows, so reconcile via provider APIs).
- **Missing webhook** means delivery stays `SENT` forever. Needs a reconciliation job and "unknown" as an honest state.
- **Failover provider reputation**: a cold provider or IP with no sending history gets throttled or spam-foldered the moment you fail over to it. It needs ongoing low-volume warmth.
- **Push**: invalid or expired tokens (must prune on APNs/FCM feedback), APNs auth key or cert expiry (a classic silent outage), and collapse-key semantics.
- **SMS**: carrier filtering, 10DLC/toll-free registration, per-country sender ID rules, and STOP/HELP keyword handling that must work at the provider and in your suppression list.

### Analytics
- **Open tracking is unreliable** (Apple Mail Privacy Protection inflates it) and **clicks are inflated** by security scanners prefetching links. Don't build product decisions on raw opens.
- **Tracking domain** failures break every link in every email. Treat it as production-critical, with TLS renewal monitoring.
- **PII in analytics**: keep identifiers pseudonymous and honor deletion requests.
- **Event loss** in the sink makes dashboards quietly wrong. Reconcile counts against the delivery state table.

### Platform
- **Region or AZ loss, queue backlog, clock skew** (affects TTL/expiry and rate-limit windows), **secrets rotation** (provider keys), **runaway cost** (SMS is expensive: a loop can burn thousands of dollars in minutes, so add spend caps per type).
- **Data deletion/export (GDPR)** across rendered snapshots, events and the warehouse.

## 4. Scaling cliffs

1. **Fan-out campaigns**: a bulk send of N users dominates everything. Isolated, throttled fan-out with its own capacity.
2. **Hot recipient partitions**: a celebrity or a broken client generating thousands of events for one user pins a partition. Per-recipient ingest caps and collapse.
3. **Top-of-hour thundering herd**: digest flush and "9am local" sends cluster on the hour or at tz boundaries. Jitter schedules and spread work.
4. **`delivery` and `delivery_event` table growth**: billions of rows in a year. Time-partition from day one, with a retention policy, cold storage in the warehouse, and no unbounded secondary indexes.
5. **Preference/profile lookup QPS**: every message needs several lookups. Needs a cache with correct invalidation, and batch fetch in fan-out.
6. **Provider rate limits and per-account quotas**: your global throughput ceiling is theirs. Needs token-bucket per provider and backpressure, not unbounded queue growth.
7. **Webhook ingest bursts**: after a big send, callbacks arrive in a compressed spike. Ingest to a log first, process asynchronously.
8. **In-app**: unread counts (counter hot keys, so use materialized or approximate counts), WebSocket connection count and reconnect storms after deploys, and broadcast fan-out-on-write cost (consider fan-out-on-read for broadcast announcements).
9. **Template render CPU** for large digests and bulk sends (pre-compile templates, cache).
10. **Redis single-key hotspots** for rate limits keyed by global or tenant. Shard counters.
11. **Operational cliff**: DLQ replays and backfills that compete with live traffic. They need their own throttle and priority.

## 5. Migration risks

1. **Undocumented behavior in the old system** (special-case suppressions, hard-coded sender rules, implicit dedupe, legal footers, retry quirks). Inventory by reading code *and* sampling production sends by type for 30 days.
2. **Duplicate or missing sends during cutover.** Migrate **per notification type**, with a single owner (old or new) at any time, controlled by a flag keyed on type (and optionally user cohort). Never both.
3. **Shadow mode**: run the new pipeline with a no-op provider and diff its decisions against what the old system actually sent. This is the best de-risking tool you have.
4. **Preference and consent migration**: preserve source and timestamp, merge duplicate/conflicting records conservatively (most restrictive wins), and import all suppressions and bounces *before* any send. Missing suppression import is a deliverability and legal incident.
5. **Deliverability regression**: new sending domain, IPs, templates or link-tracking domain resets reputation. Keep the same sending identity where possible, and ramp volume gradually.
6. **Provider-side config**: webhook URLs, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, SMS registrations, APNs/FCM credentials and topic/bundle configs, which are slow to change and easy to forget.
7. **Device token migration**: tokens tied to app bundle/sender IDs. Ensure continuity, or you lose push reach.
8. **In-flight and scheduled notifications** at cutover: drain or migrate them. Scheduled digests mid-window need explicit handling.
9. **Producer migration** across N teams: provide an SDK, a compatibility shim that accepts old calls and translates them, and a deadline for decommissioning.
10. **Rollback**: must be possible per type at every stage; data written by the new system (preferences!) must be mirrored back or the old system will act on stale data after rollback.
11. **User-visible changes**: in-app history continuity, copy changes, and new frequency caps that silently reduce notifications, which may hurt product metrics. Get product sign-off.
12. **Dual-run cost and cognitive load**: the migration will last longer than planned. Budget for it and set an explicit decommission date.

- **Security**: per-producer authN/Z with an allowed-types list, secrets in a vault with rotation, PII encryption at rest, template-edit permissions and audit log, and an approval step for changes to critical templates.

Per-type, per-channel, per-provider metrics: ingest-to-send latency (p50/p99), success, bounce, complaint, suppression rate, queue age (not just depth), and DLQ size. - **Operability**: kill switch per type, channel and provider; pause and resume; replay tool with dry-run; spend caps; load-test with a fake provider before any real send.

I haven't seen your current system, so I'm assuming a typical setup: a monolith or a few services with call-site-embedded send logic, one or two providers, and a relational DB. Where my answer would change based on your actual numbers, I flag it.

## Verdict

The target architecture is sound and standard. The risky part is "once and right." A big-bang rebuild of seven capabilities is how notification projects end up 18 months late with a dual-run period that never ends. I'd keep the **target design** as the north star but **sequence delivery** so each phase is shippable and the migration is per-notification-type, not per-system.

**Top 5 risks, in order:**
1. **Duplicate or missed sends during migration**, especially transactional ones (OTP, receipts).
2. **Losing suppression and consent state**, which creates legal exposure and sender-reputation damage.
3. **Bulk traffic starving transactional traffic** without hard isolation.
4. **Retry and failover causing duplicates or storms** during provider incidents.
5. **Undocumented business logic at call sites** that the rebuild silently drops.

## Questions that change the design

- Peak and average messages per second, per channel? Largest single fan-out (one event to N users)?
- Number of producing services and call sites?
- Latency SLO for transactional sends (OTP within 5s? 30s?)
- Single-tenant or multi-tenant? Regions and data residency?
- Regulated domain (health, finance), and which SMS countries?
- What is the actual pain in the current system? The answer determines phase 1.
- Have you evaluated buy options (Knock, Courier, Novu, SNS/Pinpoint)? The preference and policy layer is usually the part worth owning. Channel plumbing is the most commoditized.

## Target design

### Pipeline

```
Producer → [outbox] → Ingest API/bus
  → Validate + idempotency check
  → Resolve (recipient, locale, tz, channels, prefs, consent)
  → Policy (suppression, rate limit, dedupe/collapse, quiet hours, digest routing)
  → Render (pinned template version)
  → Per-channel, per-priority queues
  → Dispatcher → Provider adapter
  → Provider webhooks → Receipt ingester → Delivery events (append-only)
  → Analytics sink (off the hot path)
```

### Key decisions

**Ingestion contract.** Producers send *intents* (`type`, `recipient_id`, `payload`, `idempotency_key`, `priority`), not channel-specific payloads. Producers must not choose providers or templates. Use a transactional outbox on the producer side so "order committed but notification lost" can't happen.

**Priority isolation.** Separate queues, worker pools and provider credentials for at least two classes: *transactional/critical* and *bulk/marketing*. For email, use separate sending domains and IP pools. This is the single most important isolation boundary.

**State model.** Two levels:
- `notification` (intent) → 1..N `delivery` (one per channel/attempt)
- Deliveries are append-only events (`queued, sent, delivered, bounced, complained, failed, suppressed`) plus a derived current-state row. Don't update a hot row per webhook. Webhooks arrive out of order and duplicated, so the state machine must tolerate `delivered` before `sent`.

**Preferences and consent.**
- Model: user × category × channel, plus global and quiet-hours settings.
- Categories flagged `required` (security, legal) bypass opt-out but not hard suppression such as a bounced address.
- Keep a separate **suppression list** (hard bounces, complaints, SMS STOP, unsubscribes) that is checked at dispatch, not just at resolve time.
- Store consent as an **audit log** (who, when, source, scope), not just a boolean.
- Support RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe.

**Templates.**
- Versioned, per channel and locale, with a declared variable schema.
- Use a logic-less sandboxed engine (Liquid or Handlebars, MJML for email). No arbitrary code execution.
- Pin the template version at intent time and render as late as possible (at dispatch) so content is fresh, but store the rendered snapshot for audit and debugging.
- Need preview, test-send and lint-on-publish (missing variables, broken links).

**Digests.**
- Policy routes eligible events into a per-user, per-category pending buffer.
- A scheduler flushes by user-local window. Use a claim/lease on flush so exactly one worker owns it.
- Digests render through the same pipeline as a synthetic intent.
- Defer building this, but make sure the data model doesn't preclude it.

**Rate limiting.** Three distinct things, often conflated:
1. *Per-user frequency caps* (token bucket, per category and channel). Semantics must be defined per type: **drop, defer, or collapse**.
2. *Outbound provider throttles* (global, per provider and number).
3. *Abuse limits* (per destination and per IP, to stop SMS pumping through OTP endpoints).

**Provider layer.**
- Adapter interface: `send`, `parseWebhook`, `capabilities`, `classifyError` (retryable, permanent, throttled).
- Circuit breaker per provider, with an explicit failover policy per priority class.

**In-app.**
- Per-user inbox store with read and seen state.

- A sink provider for staging and load tests.

## Failure modes

**Ingestion**
- Producer retries create duplicates. Fix: an idempotency key with a TTL longer than the longest retry horizon.
- Idempotency store unavailable. Decide per priority whether to fail open (risk of duplicate) or closed (risk of loss). For OTP, I'd fail open.
- Poison message blocks a partition. Fix: bounded retries and a DLQ.
- Schema drift between producer and platform. Fix: schema registry and contract tests.

**Resolve and policy**
- Preference service down or stale. Define the default: send required categories, hold optional ones. Cache TTL vs. an unsubscribe that must take effect immediately: a user who unsubscribes and gets another email is a compliance issue, so invalidate on write.
- Timezone missing or wrong, so quiet hours are mis-applied. Define a fallback hierarchy (device, profile, IP-derived, account region).
- Redis rate-limit store lost, resetting all buckets and letting a burst through. Decide fail-open vs. fail-closed per category.
- Race between unsubscribe and an in-flight message. Check suppression again at dispatch, and accept that already-handed-off messages can't be recalled.
- Digest races: an event arrives mid-flush (lost or double-included); user switches digest to immediate with items pending; empty digest sent; a digest with 10,000 items (cap and summarize).
- Collapse and dedupe rules that swallow distinct events. Always log the decision.

**Render**
- Missing variable renders as blank or `{{name}}`. Fix: fail the render, never send.
- Locale fallback produces mixed-language content.
- Template version published with a bug goes out at scale. Fix: staged rollout, per-template kill switch, rollback.
- Template injection via user-supplied content (HTML injection in email, link spoofing).
- SMS encoding: one emoji switches GSM-7 to UCS-2, cutting segments from 160 to 70 characters and potentially tripling cost.

**Dispatch and providers**
- **Timeout after the provider accepted the message.** The retry then duplicates the send, and the failover provider duplicates it too. Use provider idempotency keys where supported. Otherwise accept at-least-once for email and push, and for SMS be conservative about retrying on ambiguous failures.
- Provider partial outage, with elevated latency rather than errors. Breakers need latency-based triggers, not just error rates.
- 429 handling that retries too aggressively and worsens the throttle.
- Failover provider has a different sender identity, which hurts trust and deliverability (new SMS sender IDs, email domain alignment).
- Credentials expired or rotated incorrectly (APNs keys expire, for example).
- Invalid device tokens never pruned, degrading push success metrics and APNs trust.

**Webhooks and receipts**
- Out-of-order, duplicate or missing receipts. Use idempotent event IDs and monotonic state transitions.
- Webhook endpoint down, with providers retrying for hours, then a flood. Put a thin ingest layer in front of a queue.
- Forged webhooks. Verify signatures.
- Bounce and complaint events lost, so you keep sending to bad addresses and your sender reputation decays.

**In-app**
- Unread counts drift from reality.
- Realtime connection storms after a deploy (reconnect herd).
- Inbox unbounded growth. Define retention.

**Compliance and security**
- SMS sent outside permitted hours (TCPA-style rules) or without recorded consent. STOP/HELP keywords not honored across all numbers.
- Email missing List-Unsubscribe headers (Gmail and Yahoo bulk-sender requirements).
- PII in logs, analytics and DLQs. GDPR/CCPA deletion must propagate to the inbox, delivery history, analytics and snapshots.
- Transactional content leaking through the wrong recipient mapping (a resolve bug is a data breach, so test it hard).

| Cliff | Trigger | Mitigation |

| **Bulk starving critical** | Campaign launches | Hard queue/worker/credential isolation and per-class concurrency caps. |
| **Provider throughput caps** | SES send rate, Twilio MPS per number, APNs connections | Outbound token buckets sized to provider limits. Plan for number pools and short codes in SMS. |

| **Delivery table growth** | Billions of rows, status update write amplification | Append-only events, time partitioning, TTL and archival to cold storage. Don't index everything. |
| **Webhook receipt storms** | Bulk send finishes, receipts arrive in bursts | Queue-backed ingestion, batch writes. |

## How to tell them apart: the decomposition

1. **Trace diff.** Pull traces for p99-range requests from before and after. Compare span durations by name. This shows whether added time sits in a specific dependency (third party, DB, cache), in unattributed gaps (queuing, GC, throttling, network), or in a new span (code change).
2. **Edge vs. app vs. dependency time.** The LB or proxy request time minus app time shows queueing and network before the app. App time minus child spans shows in-process delay.
3. **Slice by host, AZ, and version.** If one slice is bad, look at infrastructure or a version difference. If all are equally bad, look at a shared dependency, the DB, or the measurement.
4. **Saturation signals (USE) at each tier.** Utilization, saturation (queues, waits), and errors for CPU, memory, pool, DB connections, disk, and network. Latency rising where a queue is growing is a strong lead.
5. **Time-shape matching.** Step points to a discrete change. A ramp points to growth or a leak. A sawtooth points to GC, caches, or restarts. A periodic spike points to cron or batch jobs. A cluster at a fixed value points to a timeout or retransmit.
6. **Correlate against inputs.** Cart size, item count, payment method, promo, and region. Strong correlation means a data-dependent path, not infrastructure.

# Design Review: Onboarding Redesign

I'm reviewing from the one-line scope only, with no research, flows, or mocks, so some findings are questions the plan needs to answer.

## Verdict

**The plan is a feature inventory, not a strategy.** Each of the seven parts is reasonable, but together they compete for attention in the first session, overlap (templates, sample data, and role paths all answer "what do I see first?"), and nothing says what a successfully onboarded user looks like. I'd cut scope, sequence it, and define activation before designing anything.

## Cross-cutting issues

### 1. No activation definition
Everything depends on this. For a collaborative tool, "completed the tour" is a vanity metric. Better candidates:
- *Created a project and 3+ tasks, and invited or assigned one teammate within 7 days*
- *A second person completes a task in the workspace within 14 days*

Solo evaluators and team adopters have different activation paths. Decide which you're optimizing for, or you'll build a tour that teaches features instead of a path to value.

### 2. Missing user states
The plan seems to assume one user: a new person creating a new workspace. At least six states exist:

| State | Needs |
|---|---|
| Workspace creator/admin | Setup, templates, invite teammates |
| **Invited member** (probably your largest group) | Shortened path, context of *their* team's existing work, no workspace setup |
| Guest/external collaborator | Minimal, scoped, no upsell |
| SSO/SCIM-provisioned enterprise user | Skip signup questions, admin-defined defaults |
| Migrating from Asana/Jira/Trello/Monday | **Import**, which is the biggest missing piece in the plan |
| Returning/lapsed user | Re-entry, not first-run |

Also missing: **teammate invitation** as a first-class step. For this category it is the strongest activation predictor.

### 3. Competing surfaces on first load
Tour overlay + checklist + video + template gallery + role question is too much. Set a rule: **one primary call to action per screen, and at most one persistent helper (the checklist).**

### 4. Re-entry and control
Every part needs a "skip", "come back later", and "restart" story. Put a persistent, discoverable entry point in the help menu.

## Part-by-part review

### A. Interactive tour

**Risk:** Click-through tours have notoriously low completion, and users dismiss them to get to their work. They also break whenever the UI changes.

**Alternatives**
1. **Task-driven guidance:** "Create your first task" where the step completes only when the user actually does it. This is the best option, since it teaches by producing real value.
2. **Contextual hints:** Tooltips that fire on first encounter with a feature (first time opening board view).
3. **Rich empty states with a CTA**, so there's no overlay at all.
4. **Launchpad/hub:** The user chooses what to learn, on demand.

**Recommendation:** Keep a very short tour (3–5 steps) that is action-validated, plus contextual hints for the long tail.

**Edge cases**
- Target element missing (permissions, feature flag, plan tier, collapsed sidebar, different viewport)
- Window resize or mobile breakpoint mid-tour
- User navigates away, refreshes, or switches device. Does progress persist server-side?
- User performs a step out of order
- Localization: longer strings overflowing tooltips, RTL layouts mirroring spotlight placement
- UI redesigns silently breaking anchors. Needs automated tests and an owner.
- Concurrent surfaces: tour step vs. a modal, toast, or cookie banner
- Teaching drag-and-drop (kanban) with no alternative path

**Accessibility**
- Not a keyboard trap, but focus must move to the step content and return sensibly. Esc dismisses.
- Spotlight/dim overlays: ensure highlighted content and tooltip meet contrast. Don't block screen-reader access to the page unless a true modal (and then use proper dialog semantics).
- WCAG 2.2 **2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured:** tooltips and coach marks must not cover the focused element.
- No auto-advancing steps (2.2.1 Timing). The user controls pace.
- Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` for pulsing beacons and animated transitions.
- Any step teaching a drag action must teach the keyboard/menu alternative too.
- Announce step changes ("Step 2 of 4") to assistive tech.

### B. Templates gallery

**Overlap alert:** Templates, sample data, and role-based paths all solve "blank-slate paralysis." Pick a clear hierarchy: *role/use case → recommended templates → optional sample data.*

**Alternatives**
- Inline 3–4 recommended templates in the first-run flow rather than a full gallery destination. The gallery then lives in "New project" for later.
- AI- or prompt-generated starter structure ("Describe your project")
- Import-first for migrators

**Edge cases**
- Applying a template to an existing populated workspace (merge? new project only?)
- Templates containing assignees, dates, or automations: how do they resolve for a solo user? Relative dates are better than absolute.
- Template that references features the user's plan doesn't include
- Org-custom templates vs. global ones; permission to publish
- Zero search results; slow-loading previews; preview of a template that contains sample "people"
- Localization of template content, not just UI
- Template quality decay. Who curates?

**Accessibility**
- Cards should be real links or buttons with a single accessible name. Avoid nested interactive elements.
- Preview images need meaningful alt text or be marked decorative if the title carries the meaning.
- Filters/categories: use proper tab/radio/checkbox semantics, and announce result counts (4.1.3).
- Reflow at 320px / 400% zoom: the grid must collapse cleanly.

### C. Sample data

**Biggest hidden risk in the plan.** It's often the source of the worst downstream problems.

**Alternatives**
- Templates with placeholder tasks (clearly editable), instead of fake "people and history"
- A separate **demo project** in a sandbox, not mixed with real work
- Ghost/overlay content in empty states that disappears on first real input

**Edge cases**
- **Contamination:** sample items appearing in search, reports, "my tasks," workload views, or billing/usage counts
- **Notifications and integrations:** sample assignments must never email real people or sync to Slack/Jira/calendar
- **Invited members** joining a workspace and seeing fake data mixed with the team's real data. Never seed into a workspace with real content.
- Deleting: is it one click and total? What about items the user edited, or that others have commented on?
- Analytics: exclude sample-data actions from activation metrics, or "created a task" will be inflated
- Fake names/avatars: avoid stereotyped or culturally narrow sets, and don't impersonate real users
- API/CSV export including sample data
- Sample data in a non-English workspace

**Accessibility**
- Mark sample content with a visible, text-based label ("Sample"), not just color or opacity. Make sure it's exposed to screen readers.
- Dimmed "ghost" styling must still meet contrast requirements.

### D. Role-based paths

**Alternatives**
- Ask for *use case/team type* (software, marketing, ops) rather than job role. It predicts which templates and views matter more reliably.
- Infer from email domain, invite context, or the inviter's workspace, and ask nothing.
- Progressive profiling: one question up front, the rest later.

**Edge cases**
- Wrong choice or changed mind. Make it editable in settings.
- Multi-role users (founder who is admin, PM, and contributor)
- Role in your taxonomy ≠ permission role in the product. Conflating them is confusing: "Manager" path vs. "Admin" permission.
- "Other"/"Skip" must lead to a decent default, not a degraded experience
- Path-specific content drifting out of sync (N roles × M steps maintenance)
- Permissions: a contributor's path must not tell them to do things they can't (invite, create workspace-level templates)

**Accessibility**
- Role selection as a radio group or large labeled buttons with visible focus, not image-only tiles
- Don't use illustrations or icons as the sole label
- Plain, jargon-free role descriptions (3.1.5-style reading-level consideration)
- Don't ask for the same info the user already gave at signup (3.3.7 Redundant Entry)

### E. Progress checklist

**Alternatives**
- Checklist as the sole persistent element (recommended) vs. a one-time setup wizard vs. a "getting started" page

**Design guidance:** 4–6 items, ordered by value (not feature coverage), auto-completed by detecting real actions, collapsible, dismissible, with a clear end state.

**Edge cases**
- User completed items before first seeing the checklist (pre-check them)
- Item completed and then undone (deleted the project): does the check revert?
- Item impossible for this user (permission, plan tier, no teammates yet). Hide or adapt rather than leaving a permanently stuck item.
- Cross-device and cross-session persistence; per-user vs. per-workspace state (the invite item shouldn't re-appear for every new member)
- Dismissed by accident. Offer an undo path.
- Completion celebration: don't block, and keep it proportionate
- What happens at 100%? What if the user never finishes? Auto-retire after N days.
- Floating widget overlapping content on small screens or in dense board views

**Accessibility**
- Progress as text ("3 of 5 complete"), not just a ring or bar. Use `progressbar` semantics with a value, or a plain text equivalent.
- Item completion announced via polite live region (4.1.3). No focus stealing.
- Floating checklist mustn't obscure focused content (2.4.11) or cause horizontal scroll at 400% zoom.
- Completed state indicated by more than green color (icon + text, e.g. "Completed")
- Minimum 24×24 CSS px targets (2.5.8)

### F. In-app video

**Alternatives**
- Short (≤60–90s) looped muted clips for specific interactions; screenshot walkthroughs; written step guides; a searchable help panel. Video is often the *least* scannable format and the most expensive to maintain.

**Recommendation:** Use video sparingly, for concepts that are hard to show statically (e.g. views and automations). Never make it required for any checklist item.

**Edge cases**
- Blocked by corporate firewalls or CSP; third-party hosts raising privacy/consent issues (e.g. embedded YouTube cookies)
- Bandwidth/data constraints; mobile autoplay behavior
- Videos go stale after each UI change, and nobody owns updating them
- Localization (subtitles vs. re-recording), and video language vs. UI language
- Autoplay in a shared office
- Video completion counted as "learned" in metrics

**Accessibility (the most compliance-heavy part)**
- Accurate captions (1.2.2) and a full transcript. Audio description or equivalent narration if visuals carry information (1.2.5, or 1.2.3 as a minimum).
- **No autoplay with sound.** Any looping or moving content >5s needs pause/stop/hide (2.2.2).
- Fully keyboard-operable, labeled player controls; test with the specific player you embed.
- Avoid flashing content (2.3.1), and honor reduced motion.
- Don't put critical instructions *only* in video.

### G. Success-metrics dashboard

**Fundamental ambiguity:** Is this an internal analytics dashboard or a customer-facing admin feature? They're completely different projects. If internal, it's instrumentation, not onboarding design, and it likely belongs in your existing BI tool. If customer-facing ("team adoption" for admins), it's a product feature that needs its own design.

**Alternatives**
- Use your existing analytics/BI stack and spend the effort on a clean event taxonomy, rather than building a bespoke dashboard.
- Start with a weekly review of 5 numbers.

**What to measure**
- *Primary:* activation rate (per your definition), time-to-activation
- *Funnel:* drop-off per step; role-selection completion; template chosen vs. blank; invite sent/accepted
- *Engagement with aids:* tour skip/complete, checklist item completion, video watch rate. These are diagnostic, not success measures.
- *Outcome:* D7/D30 retention, team-size growth, paid conversion
- *Guardrails:* support tickets, time-to-first-task (must not get *worse*), rage clicks, dismiss-at-step-1 rate, accessibility-related feedback

**Edge cases**
- Segmenting by user state (creator vs. invitee). Blended averages will mislead you.
- Excluding sample data, internal/test accounts, and bots
- Consent/privacy (GDPR/CCPA), and not logging free-text
- Attribution: you can't conclude cause without a **holdout/A-B test**. Otherwise you'll credit onboarding for seasonal shifts.
- Small cohorts for enterprise, so use qualitative methods there
- Baseline: capture current-state metrics *before* shipping

**Accessibility (if customer-facing)**
- Charts need text alternatives or data tables, patterns beyond color, and keyboard-accessible tooltips. Avoid hover-only data.

## Cross-cutting accessibility checklist (WCAG 2.2 AA)

- Whole flow completable by keyboard alone; logical focus order; visible focus
- Every overlay: correct dialog semantics, focus management on open/close, Esc to dismiss, nothing obscuring focus
- No time limits or auto-advance; no motion without a pause control and reduced-motion support
- Status updates via live regions, without stealing focus
- Contrast ≥4.5:1 text and ≥3:1 UI components, including dimmed and "ghost" states
- Reflow to 320px/400% zoom; text spacing overrides don't break tooltips
- Plain language; consistent help location (3.2.6); don't make users re-enter data
- Mobile: touch targets, orientation, and whether the tour even applies
- **Test with actual screen readers (NVDA/JAWS + VoiceOver) and keyboard-only users**, not just automated scans, which catch roughly a third of issues
- Recruit users with disabilities for usability testing

## Recommended sequencing

| Phase | Scope | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **0 – Foundations** | Define activation; instrument current funnel; baseline metrics; map user states; interview 8–10 recent signups and churned trials | You can't judge improvement without it |
| **1 – Core path** | Use-case question (1–2 Qs) → recommended templates → (optional, labeled) sample data → invite teammates → 5-item checklist; **import** for migrators; short invitee path | Highest value per unit of effort |
| **2 – Guidance** | 3–5 step action-validated tour; contextual hints; selective captioned video | Add only what Phase 1 data shows is needed |
| **3 – Measurement UI** | Dashboard (or just BI reports); customer-facing adoption view if validated | Lowest user impact |

Run Phase 1 against a holdout.

## Open questions to resolve
1. What is the activation event, and what's the current baseline?
2. What share of new users are invitees vs. workspace creators?
3. Is the dashboard internal or customer-facing?
4. Is there an import path today? Should it be part of this plan?
5. Who owns ongoing maintenance of tour anchors, templates, and videos?
6. Does mobile need onboarding, or is it desktop-first?
7. What localization commitments exist?
8. What does the current drop-off data say about *where* people leave?

# Design Review: Onboarding Redesign for a Project-Management Tool

## Verdict

The parts are individually reasonable, but the plan lists seven features and no strategy. It doesn't say what "activated" means, who the users are, or how the pieces interact. A tour, a checklist, templates, sample data, videos, and role paths all compete for the same first-session attention. Shipping all seven at once is the main risk, because you couldn't tell which one moved the numbers.

**Recommendation:** define activation first, then build the smallest coherent path to it (templates, sample data, checklist). Layer the tour, role paths, and video in behind experiments. Build the metrics dashboard first, because you need it to judge everything else.

---

## 0. Gaps to resolve before design starts

| Question | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| What is the activation event? (e.g., "created a project, added 3 tasks, invited 1 teammate, and a task was completed within 7 days") | Every component should map to it. Without one, the checklist becomes arbitrary. |
| Who arrives, and how? (self-serve signup, invited teammate, admin-provisioned enterprise, migrating from Asana/Jira/Trello) | Invited users are often the majority in collaboration tools and need a very different first run than workspace creators. |
| Is the product single-player-useful, or only valuable with a team? | Determines whether the "aha" is personal (my tasks organized) or social (team sees shared status). |
| Where do users drop off today? | The redesign should target the worst funnel step, not the most fun feature. |
| Platforms: web only, or mobile and desktop too? | The tour, video, and checklist all behave differently on small screens. |

---

## 1. Interactive tour

**Risk:** Tours are the most commonly skipped onboarding element. Users want to do something, not watch something, and tours do poorly when they front-load every feature.

**Alternatives**
- **A. Linear modal/tooltip tour** (the default): cheap, but low retention.
- **B. Task-driven tour:** the user performs real actions ("Create your first task") and the UI advances on completion. Higher engagement, and it doubles as activation.
- **C. Contextual, just-in-time hints:** a small tip appears the first time the user opens Board view or Automations. There is no up-front tour at all.
- **D. Empty states as onboarding:** each empty screen explains and offers the primary action.

**Recommendation:** B for the core loop (3–5 steps max), then C for everything else. D is nearly free and should be done regardless.

**Edge cases**
- User skips, then wants it back: provide a persistent "Replay tour" in the Help menu.
- User navigates away mid-tour or refreshes: persist the step server-side, not in local state.
- Target element missing (permissions, feature flag, different plan, role path): the step must degrade or skip, never dead-end.
- UI changes after ship (anchors break): use stable data attributes and test the tour in CI.
- Viewport too small, or the tooltip overlaps the target or goes off-screen.
- Invited user lands in a workspace with existing content: "Create your first project" is wrong for them.
- Browser back button, deep links, and multi-tab behavior.
- Localization: longer strings overflow tooltips, and RTL needs mirrored placement.

**Accessibility**
- Treat spotlight overlays as dialogs: move focus into the tooltip, trap or manage focus properly, and restore focus on close.
- Esc closes it, and there is always a visible "Skip" with a real button role.
- Don't rely on dimmed overlay and color alone. Announce step changes ("Step 2 of 5") via `aria-live` or heading focus.
- No auto-advancing on a timer (WCAG 2.2.1), and honor `prefers-reduced-motion` for spotlight animations.
- Ensure the highlighted element stays operable by keyboard and isn't obscured by the tooltip (WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured).
- Tooltips need to survive 200–400% zoom and reflow.

---

## 2. Templates gallery

**Risk:** A big gallery creates choice paralysis. Quality varies, and templates users don't understand become clutter they have to delete.

**Alternatives**
- **A. Browsable gallery** with categories and search.
- **B. Question-led recommendation:** "What are you managing?" yields 3 suggested templates. This pairs naturally with role paths.
- **C. AI/prompt-generated starter project** ("Plan a product launch"): highest personalization, but needs quality control and a fallback.
- **D. Import from an existing tool** as a first-class option. For switchers, this beats any template.

**Recommendation:** B as the default, with A reachable via "Browse all", plus D if switching is a significant acquisition source. Treat C as a later experiment.

**Edge cases**
- Template preview before committing, and a clear way to undo after applying.
- Applying a template into an existing project versus creating a new one.
- Template includes assignees, dates, or automations that reference users or integrations that don't exist. Define the behavior (strip, placeholder, prompt).
- Dates: relative to today or to a chosen start date? Stale hard-coded dates look broken.
- Template adoption by a user without create permissions.
- Gallery load failure or slow network: skeleton states and a "Start blank" fallback that is always visible.
- Plan-gated templates: show them labeled, not as a surprise paywall after click.
- Ownership and maintenance: who updates templates when features change?

**Accessibility**
- The gallery is a list or grid of cards: use real buttons or links with descriptive names ("Product launch template, 12 tasks"), not click-handler divs.
- Preview images need meaningful alt text or should be marked decorative, with the description in text.
- Category filters should be a labeled group with a clear selected state (not color-only), and announce result counts on filter change.
- Preview modals follow dialog focus rules.

---

## 3. Sample data

**Risk:** Sample data makes an empty product feel alive, but it can pollute real workspaces, skew analytics, confuse teammates, and teach users to ignore content.

**Alternatives**
- **A. Pre-populated sample project** that is clearly labeled and deletable.
- **B. Ghost or demo mode:** sample content that is visually distinct and disappears upon first real action.
- **C. Interactive sandbox** separate from the real workspace.
- **D. No sample data:** rely on good templates and empty states.

**Recommendation:** A with strong labeling, or B if engineering permits. Make sample data one click to remove, and remove it automatically when the user creates real content, with a prompt.

**Edge cases**
- **Teammates see it:** if one person adds sample data to a shared workspace, everyone sees it. Scope it to the individual, or mark it visibly as sample.
- **Notifications, emails, and integrations:** sample tasks must never trigger real notifications, assignees, or calendar syncs.
- **Analytics contamination:** exclude sample objects from usage metrics, billing counts, and quotas. This is critical for the success dashboard.
- **Search and reporting:** sample items appearing in search, @-mentions, or workspace reports.
- Deleting a sample project that the user has already edited: warn, since they may have started using it.
- Users who never delete it: define an expiry or reminder.
- Sample data and localization: names, dates, and content should localize.
- API and export: sample items shouldn't leak into CSV exports or webhooks.

**Accessibility**
- A "Sample" label must be programmatic text, not just a colored badge.
- Don't let sample content mislead screen reader users. Include "(sample)" in the accessible name of the project.
- Sample illustrations and avatars should be decorative or properly labeled.

---

## 4. Role-based paths

**Risk:** Self-reported roles are often wrong or ambiguous. Paths multiply content maintenance and QA, and a wrong guess can hide features users need. It also adds a question before the user sees any value.

**Alternatives**
- **A. Role question at signup** (PM, designer, engineer, marketer, exec).
- **B. Goal- or use-case-based question** ("What do you want to do first?"). This is usually a better predictor of needs than job title.
- **C. Inferred from context:** invite source, email domain, referral campaign, or first actions.
- **D. Single path with progressive personalization:** adapt after observing behavior.

**Recommendation:** B, limited to 3–5 options, skippable, and used only to choose templates and checklist items. Keep the underlying product identical. Always allow switching later via settings.

**Edge cases**
- User fits multiple roles, or none ("Other" must be a first-class option).
- Invited users: use the inviter's context, or ask a shorter version. Admins versus members versus guests/viewers need different paths based on permissions, not self-label.
- Role selected, then user changes their mind or job: provide a settings entry to switch.
- Role-specific features gated by plan or permission.
- Skip rate: if more than ~30–40% skip, the question is costing you more than it gives.
- Privacy and data use: be transparent about why you ask. Check regulatory constraints on profiling in some regions.
- Content debt: each path multiplies copy, assets, and translation.

**Accessibility**
- Option cards should be a radio group (single select) or checkbox group (multi), with a visible label and fieldset legend, not custom click targets.
- Selected state must not depend on color alone.
- Avoid job-title jargon that excludes non-native speakers. Add short descriptions.

---

## 5. Progress checklist

**Risk:** A checklist can create motivation (goal-gradient effect) or feel like homework. Tasks that don't tie to real value, or that can't be completed, undermine trust.

**Alternatives**
- **A. Persistent sidebar or widget checklist** (common pattern).
- **B. Dedicated "Getting started" home page** that disappears after completion.
- **C. Inline next-best-action prompt**, showing one step at a time rather than a list.
- **D. Milestone-based** ("Set up", "Collaborate", "Automate") rather than individual tasks.

**Recommendation:** A with 4–6 items, each tied to the activation path. Auto-detect completion from real actions, never require users to tick boxes manually. Provide dismiss and re-open.

**Edge cases**
- Items already completed before the checklist appears (e.g., invited user who already has tasks): auto-check them.
- Items that depend on permission ("Invite teammates" for a guest): hide or replace them.
- Completion detection lag or failure: the user did the thing and it isn't checked. This is a trust-breaker.
- Undoing the action (deleting the task): does the check revert? Decide and document.
- Users who dismiss it and later want it back.
- 100% completion: celebrate briefly, then retire. Don't leave a permanent "100%" widget.
- Checklist overlapping the tour: two systems guiding the same action simultaneously. Make the tour update the checklist and vice versa, so they share state.
- Multi-workspace users: is progress per user or per workspace?
- Team-level versus individual-level items (the team checklist is distinct from the personal one).

**Accessibility**
- Use a real list with accessible state ("Completed" / "Not completed") as text, not just a checkmark icon.
- The progress indicator should be a `progressbar` role with value text ("3 of 5 steps completed"), not a purely visual ring.
- Announce completion politely (`aria-live="polite"`), without stealing focus.
- Confetti or animation: provide reduced-motion alternatives and never flash more than three times per second.
- The collapsed or expanded widget needs `aria-expanded`, and must not cover content at narrow widths or high zoom.

---

## 6. In-app video

**Risk:** Video is expensive to produce, goes stale quickly as the UI changes, is hard to localize, and is often skipped. It is also the component most likely to create accessibility failures.

**Alternatives**
- **A. Embedded videos** in a help panel or checklist.
- **B. Short looping GIF/MP4 clips** (5–10 seconds) inside tooltips or empty states, demonstrating a single action.
- **C. Interactive walkthroughs** (Arcade/Navattic-style) that stay in sync with the real UI.
- **D. Written, illustrated mini-guides** with optional video.

**Recommendation:** One short (under 90 seconds) welcome video at most, optional, plus B-style clips for specific features. Prefer text and in-product guidance for everything procedural. Reserve video for conveying *why*, not *how*.

**Edge cases**
- Slow, metered, or blocked networks (corporate firewalls blocking YouTube/Vimeo): use a poster image, a retry, and a text fallback.
- Autoplay with sound: don't.
- Third-party embed privacy and cookie consent obligations.
- Videos going stale after UI changes: assign an owner and a review cadence, and put a version or date in the metadata.
- Localization: subtitles at minimum, and dubbing or localized versions if the market warrants it.
- Mobile data usage and picture-in-picture behavior.
- Tracking: measure plays, completion, and whether viewers go on to complete the related checklist item.

**Accessibility**
- Captions are required (WCAG 1.2.2), and an audio description or a text-equivalent transcript where visuals carry information (1.2.3/1.2.5).
- Accessible player controls: keyboard operable, labeled, visible focus. Verify any third-party player.
- No autoplay, and any looping clips over 5 seconds need a pause control (WCAG 2.2.2). Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` by showing a static frame.
- Provide a transcript or text summary next to the video.
- Avoid flashing content, and ensure sufficient contrast for burned-in text.

## 7. Success-metrics dashboard

**First, clarify the audience.** The plan doesn't say. Options:
- **Internal (product/growth team):** funnel and experiment results.
- **Customer admin:** "How is our team adopting the tool?"
- **End user:** a personal progress view (overlaps with the checklist).

Each is a different product. If internal, this is analytics infrastructure rather than UI design, and it should be built **first**, not last.

**Alternatives**
- **A. Use existing BI/product analytics** (Amplitude, Mixpanel, a warehouse with Looker/Metabase) rather than building a custom dashboard.
- **B. Custom in-app admin adoption dashboard**, which is a customer-facing feature and has its own value.
- **C. Lightweight weekly digest** instead of a dashboard.

**Recommendation:** A for internal use now. Treat B as a separate, later product decision.

**Metrics to define**
- Primary: activation rate (as defined in §0), time-to-first-value, and day-7/day-30 retention.
- Funnel: signup → role/goal answered → first project → first task → invite sent → invite accepted → collaborative action.
- Per-component: tour start/complete/skip, template picked vs. blank start, sample data deleted vs. retained, checklist item completion, video play/complete.
- Guardrails: support tickets, time to first action, rage clicks, and error rates.
- Segment by acquisition source, role/goal, invited vs. creator, platform, and plan.

**Edge cases and pitfalls**
- Sample data and test accounts polluting the numbers (see §3).
- Attribution: when everything ships together, you can't attribute the lift. Hence feature flags and holdouts.
- Small sample sizes for per-role breakdowns.
- Survivorship bias in completion metrics (only people who finish are counted).
- Vanity metrics: checklist completion rate going up doesn't mean activation did.
- Consent: event tracking must respect cookie and privacy settings and regional regulations, and tracking must be done consistently across clients.
- Data latency, and event schema changes breaking historical comparability.

**Accessibility (if user- or admin-facing)**
- Charts need text alternatives or data tables, patterns/labels in addition to color, and keyboard-accessible tooltips.
- Don't encode trend direction by red/green alone.

## 8. Cross-cutting concerns

**Coherence and sequencing.** Suggested first-session flow: sign-up → (optional) one goal question → template or import recommendation → workspace opens with the template and, optionally, sample data → task-driven mini-tour of the core action → checklist appears with the first items already checked. The video is available in the help panel or empty states, not forced. Make sure only one guidance layer is active at a time, with a single shared state store (tour, checklist, and hints should all read from the same "onboarding progress" model).

**Invited users and teams.** Likely the most underserved group. They need a path oriented around "what's the team already doing and what's mine?" (assigned tasks, how to comment, how to update status), not creating projects from scratch.

**Returning and lapsed users.** Someone who signs up, leaves, and returns 10 days later should resume intelligently, not restart or see nothing.

**Existing users.** Decide whether current users see any of this. Surprise tours for people who've used the product for two years are annoying. Offer opt-in discovery ("What's new") instead.

**Admin and enterprise.** SSO or SCIM-provisioned users may land without ever seeing signup. Admins may want to disable or customize onboarding, set default templates, and suppress sample data. Consider compliance and security review needs for third-party tooling (tour libraries, video hosts).

**Mobile and responsive.** Tours with anchored tooltips often break on small screens. Decide whether mobile gets a reduced path, with checklist and templates only.

**Performance.** Third-party tour and video scripts affect load time on the critical first screen. Lazy-load them.

**Localization and RTL.** Plan string expansion, templates by locale, and caption translation up front.

**Failure and offline states.** Every network-dependent component (gallery, video, checklist sync) needs a skeleton, an error state, and a "continue without" path.

**Global accessibility baseline (WCAG 2.2 AA)**
- Full keyboard operability and logical focus order across every overlay, widget, and card.
- Visible focus indicators and ≥ 4.5:1 text contrast (3:1 for UI components).
- Target size ≥ 24×24 CSS px (2.5.8).
- Don't block copy/paste or zoom.
- Screen-reader testing with at least NVDA+Firefox/Chrome and VoiceOver+Safari, and test with 200% zoom and Windows High Contrast.
- Timing: nothing auto-dismisses without user control.
- Cognitive accessibility: plain language, short steps, and the ability to skip, pause, and resume without penalty.
- Ensure onboarding overlays don't trap users who rely on assistive tech, and that dismissing them is always possible.

## 9. Suggested phasing

| Phase | Scope | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | Define activation. Instrument the funnel. Set up the internal dashboard (using existing tools). Fix empty states. | You can't evaluate anything else without it, and empty states are cheap and high-value. |
| **1** | Goal question (skippable), template recommendations + "start blank", labeled removable sample data, auto-detecting checklist | Shortest path to a populated, meaningful workspace. |
| **2** | Task-driven mini-tour for the core loop, invited-user path | Add guidance once content and checklist exist. |
| **3** | Contextual hints, short clips, optional welcome video, import flow | Depth, after learning what users struggle with. |
| **4** | Role/goal-based personalization refinement, AI-generated starters, customer-facing adoption dashboard | Only if Phase 1–3 data justifies it. |

Run each phase behind feature flags with a holdout group so results are attributable.
